title: Annis Mound & Village
summary: In Butler County, Annis was a Mississippian mound center with a platform mound inside a palisaded village, dated by the state to the early to mid-1300s.
bodyMarkdown:
The Annis Mound and Village site is a Mississippian mound center in Butler County with a platform mound inside a palisaded village. The village was enlarged several times. Two major excavations, decades apart, have made it one of the better-understood Mississippian towns in Kentucky.

## Excavations

The [Kentucky Archaeological Survey's Annis page](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Annis.aspx) says the University of Kentucky dug the site from February 1939 to April 1940 as a Works Progress Administration project. Pennsylvania State University returned for more work in the summers of 2002 to 2004. An account of the [Annis Mound and Village site](https://grokipedia.com/page/annis_mound_and_village_site) adds an earlier visit by Clarence B. Moore in 1916 and names W. S. Webb and Scott Hammerstedt among the archaeologists.

The work found three palisades, 17 structures with related features and a platform mound. The mound measured 110 feet on a side and stood 12 feet tall. Each palisade was larger than the one before and enclosed a bigger village. Only the last and largest had bastions, and the village it enclosed covered about 4.5 acres.

## Dates

The sources disagree on when the town was occupied. The archaeology survey dates the village and mound to the early to mid-1300s AD. Another account gives a much longer span, from about 800 CE to about 1300 CE. Readers should treat the dates as unsettled. Both agree the mound and palisades belong to the Mississippian period.

## A changing center

The survey describes how the town's use of the mound shifted. At first a local leader persuaded others to build a low platform mound and a small palisade, and he lived on top of the mound. Later the summit held a large public building inside a fence, probably for ritual. The chief then seems to have lived close to the mound, and a second, larger palisade went up.

In the final phase the mound was greatly enlarged and again became the chief's home. Archaeologists suggest this may have been a new, perhaps unrelated leader using the mound to claim authority. The bastioned palisade may point to local social stress, a show of the chief's power or both.

The villagers grew maize as a staple and made typical Mississippian pottery. A few sherds of high-status pottery from Cahokia turned up in the mound-top building.

## The work of building

Archaeologists used experiments to estimate the labor involved. With 50 workers on five-hour days, the first mound stage could have taken as many as 5.5 days and the last as many as 23. The smallest palisade could have taken up to 14 days and the largest up to 33.

## Kentucky today

A 9-acre area was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1985. The much older Annis Sand Mound, an Archaic period feature, lies outside the palisade. Annis is a different site from the [Carlston Annis Shell Mound](/stories/carlston-annis-shell-mound/). This story gives the county only. The site was home to Native families and deserves respect.
